phase1.intro:
Every control you met last lesson has been inert. This lesson is where the storefront starts responding to the customer.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: How does setOnAction() actually work with lambdas?
dialogue: [[term:setOnAction()]] takes an [[term:EventHandler]] — a [[term:functional interface]] (one abstract method, handle(ActionEvent e)) — so you can hand it a lambda instead: `button.setOnAction(e -> label.setText("Clicked!"))`. [[key:That's the same lambda syntax you used for Comparator and Runnable back in Unit 4]].

stickyNote.flavor: ⚡ EventHandler is functional — lambdas fit right in
stickyNote.definition: setOnAction() takes an EventHandler (a functional interface), so a lambda like e -> label.setText(...) works directly, same as Comparator/Runnable.

topics.buttonText: What if I need to react to more than just a click?
dialogue: TextField has `setOnAction()` too (fires on Enter), but for continuous typing you'd listen to its `textProperty()` instead — a property listener fires on every keystroke, not just once. Checkboxes typically get watched the same way, through their own *Property() listener.

stickyNote.flavor: ⌨️ every keystroke, not just Enter or a click
stickyNote.definition: setOnAction() fires once per click or Enter. A *Property() listener (like textProperty()) fires continuously, e.g. on every keystroke.

topics.buttonText: Can I have multiple handlers on the same control?
dialogue: [[warn:One handler per control]] — calling setOnAction() a second time on the same button replaces the first handler, it doesn't add a second one. If you need multiple things to happen on one click, they all belong inside the same lambda body.

stickyNote.definition: Calling setOnAction() again on the same control replaces the previous handler rather than adding a second one — combine logic in one lambda.

phase1.output: (Window with interactive controls that update the label when events occur)
phase1.openingDialogue: setOnAction() takes a lambda and makes a control actually respond — but calling it twice replaces the handler, it doesn't stack. ⚡

phase2.errorMessage: (Button appears but does NOTHING when clicked — no error, just silent failure!)
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:the button appears, looks perfectly normal, and does absolutely nothing when clicked]] — no error anywhere, which is exactly what makes this bug annoying to track down.

The button was constructed, styled, and added to the layout — every visual step is correct. [[key:what's missing is the one line that actually wires behavior to the click]]: button.setOnAction(...). Without it, the Button is a fully functional UI control that simply has no opinion about what a click should do, so JavaFX does the only reasonable thing: nothing.

phase3.openingDialogue: Events make your UI come alive! ⚡

mcq.question:
Why can button.setOnAction(e -> ...) take a lambda instead of a full anonymous EventHandler class?

A) setOnAction() is a special JavaFX-only keyword that always accepts lambdas
B) EventHandler is a functional interface — one abstract method — so a lambda can implement it directly
C) Lambdas are only allowed inside JavaFX event methods
D) ActionEvent extends Runnable, which supports lambdas

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a JavaFX program with:
1. A TextField for user input
2. A Button "Submit"
3. A Label that displays the text entered

When the button is clicked, the label should update with "Hello, [text]!"
When the user presses Enter in the TextField, the label should also update.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:calling setOnAction() twice on the same button doesn't stack handlers]] — the second call silently replaces the first. If you genuinely need more than one independent reaction to the same click, JavaFX's lower-level addEventHandler() (unlike setOnAction) can attach multiple handlers to the same event type without overwriting each other.
